definitions.meaning: A circuit building block that takes one or two binary inputs and produces one binary output by a fixed rule.
A gate whose output is 1 only when both of its inputs are 1.
A gate whose output is 1 when either input (or both) is 1.
A gate with one input whose output flips it: 1 becomes 0 and 0 becomes 1.
A binary signal, 0 or 1, fed into a gate; here the inputs are A, B and C.
The binary signal a gate produces; the OR gate output is the alarm signal here.
A table listing the output for every combination of inputs, filled in row by row.
Gates connected by wires so the output of one gate can feed the input of another.
The 0 or 1 value travelling along a wire from one part of the circuit to the next.

mechanismSteps: Meet the circuit: inputs A and B feed the AND gate, C feeds the NOT gate, and both gate outputs meet at the OR gate driving the alarm (s1).
The AND path: with A and B both 1 the AND output is 1, passes through OR and lights the alarm; truth table row 1 1 1 gives alarm 1 (s2).
Both paths zero: with B at 0 the AND output is 0 and with C at 1 NOT C is 0, so the OR output and the alarm stay 0 (s3).
The NOT path: with C at 0, NOT C is 1, and that single 1 through the OR gate lights the alarm even though the AND output is 0 (s4).
objectives: Describe the circuit alarm = (A AND B) OR (NOT C) and what each gate does
Evaluate the AND and NOT gates before the OR gate for any input combination
Fill in the truth table row by row from the gate outputs
subject: computing
title: Logic gates: one circuit, alarm = (A AND B) OR (NOT C)

trap.explanation: The slip: Both gates seem to pass a signal onward, so OR and AND blur into one rule and the NOT on C is easy to overlook. The fix: Read the circuit gate by gate: the alarm is on only when (A AND B) are both 1 or NOT C is 1 - that is, when A and B are both on, or C is off (or both). In class, replay scene 3: freeze the circuit at A=1, B=0, C=1 and ask what each gate outputs - AND gives 0 and NOT gives 0, so ask how the alarm could possibly be on; it cannot, so A alone never decides it.
trap.misconception: The alarm is on whenever A is on, because OR works just like AND.

workedExample: Test the A-alone claim on this circuit. Step 1 (s3): take the row A=1, B=0, C=1, where the claim predicts alarm 1. Step 2: evaluate gate by gate - the AND output is 0 because B is 0, and NOT C is 0 because C is 1. Step 3: the OR of 0 and 0 is 0, so the alarm stays off. So the alarm follows the gate-by-gate rule, never input A alone.
